prompt: Ana moves the `aws_vpc.shop` block out of `main.tf` into a new file, `network.tf`, in the same directory, and runs `terraform plan`. What does the plan propose?
hint: How does Terraform read a directory?

choices.text: To replace the VPC, because the block now lives in a different file
choices.why: The file a block sits in is not part of its identity; the address `aws_vpc.shop` is.

choices.text: No changes: the address is what identifies the VPC
choices.why: Right. Every `.tf` file in the directory is one document, and file names mean nothing to Terraform.

choices.text: A second VPC, created from `network.tf`
choices.why: There is still one block with that address; moving it does not copy it.

choices.text: It ignores `network.tf` until `versions.tf` lists it
choices.why: No file lists the others: every `.tf` file in the directory is read.

prompt: In `resource "aws_vpc" "shop"`, what is `shop`?
hint: One of the two labels is defined by the provider, the other by you.

choices.text: The resource type, which the AWS provider defines
choices.why: The type is the first label, `aws_vpc`.

choices.text: The VPC's `Name` tag in AWS
choices.why: The tag is an argument inside the block; it happens to say `shop` too, and could say anything.

choices.text: The id AWS will give the VPC
choices.why: AWS invents the id at creation; nobody writes it in a file.

choices.text: A name chosen by Ana, used in the address `aws_vpc.shop`
choices.why: Yes. Type plus name is the address the rest of the configuration uses.

prompt: Match each block to what it does in Ana's configuration.
hint: Three blocks, three jobs, and one job no block does.

pairs.right: Names the plugins the configuration needs, and which versions
Configures the plugin, here with a region
Asks for one thing to exist

right_distractors: Holds the access key and secret for AWS

prompt: What does `terraform init` create in the AWS account?
hint: It prepares a directory.

choices.text: The resources in the configuration, without asking
choices.why: Creating resources is apply's job, and apply asks first.

choices.text: No resource at all
choices.why: Right. It installs providers into `.terraform/` and writes the lock file; AWS is not touched.

choices.text: A test resource to check the credentials
choices.why: init does not even need credentials; it never calls AWS.

choices.text: An empty state file in a bucket
choices.why: In this lesson the state is a local file, and the first apply writes it.

prompt: Ana is about to make her first commit. Which of these belong in the repository? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them is 789M and rebuilt by a command.

choices.text: `.terraform.lock.hcl`
choices.why: Yes: it makes every init, anywhere, choose the same provider versions.

choices.text: `.terraform/`
choices.why: That is the provider program itself; `init` rebuilds it, so it is ignored.

choices.text: `main.tf`
choices.why: Yes, it is the description itself.

choices.text: `versions.tf`
choices.why: Yes; it says which providers and versions the configuration accepts.

choices.text: `terraform.tfstate`
choices.why: Ana's `.gitignore` excludes it; lesson 7 says where it belongs instead.

prompt: Ana commits the lock file from the lab, which holds a single `h1:` hash for `linux_amd64`. A colleague on a Mac runs `terraform init`. What happens?
hint: The warning init printed said which platforms the file covers.

choices.text: init recomputes the hash for macOS and continues quietly
choices.why: A lock file exists to refuse a package it cannot match; it does not trust a new one silently.

choices.text: init installs the Linux package, which runs on the Mac
choices.why: A provider is a compiled program for one platform; the Linux build does not run on macOS.

choices.text: init fails: no hash matches the Mac's package
choices.why: Right. The warning said so, and `terraform providers lock` with internet access adds the other platforms.

choices.text: init ignores the lock file and picks the newest 6.x
choices.why: Only `init -upgrade` chooses again; a plain init honours the lock file.

prompt: Why does Ana not need to tell Terraform that the subnet must be created after the VPC?
hint: Look at what the subnet's `vpc_id` is set to.

choices.text: Because the VPC block comes first in `main.tf`
choices.why: The order of blocks in the file is ignored.

choices.text: Because Terraform creates resources in alphabetical order of type
choices.why: The plan is printed in alphabetical order; creation follows the graph, and the security group came before the rule regardless of names.

choices.text: The reference `aws_vpc.shop.id` is the dependency
choices.why: Yes. A reference carries its dependency with its value, and the graph is built from references.

choices.text: Because the AWS API refuses subnets until a VPC exists, and Terraform retries
choices.why: There is no retry loop here: the subnet is not even started until the VPC's id exists.

prompt: In `vpc_id = aws_vpc.shop.id`, the `id` is not a value Ana set; it is one the VPC has once it exists. Values of that kind are called ___.
hint: The opposite of an argument.

prompt: Ana gives a subnet the range `10.30.1.0/24` inside the VPC `10.20.0.0/16`. `terraform validate` says the configuration is valid. What happens at apply?
hint: Which program knows the rule about ranges?

choices.text: AWS rejects the subnet
choices.why: Right. validate checks that the configuration is coherent; only the API knows a subnet must fit inside its VPC.

choices.text: The subnet is created, since validate already passed
choices.why: Valid means coherent, not accepted.

choices.text: Terraform widens the VPC's range so the subnet fits
choices.why: Terraform does not rewrite your arguments; it creates what you declared or fails.

choices.text: The plan refuses it before apply asks the question
choices.why: The plan does not call the API to create anything, so the range is only checked when the subnet is created.

prompt: In the first plan, the security group's `vpc_id` shows `(known after apply)` although `main.tf` sets it. Why?
hint: What is it set to?

choices.text: Ana forgot to set it
choices.why: It is set, to `aws_vpc.shop.id`.

choices.text: It is the VPC's id, and the VPC does not exist yet
choices.why: Yes. A plan is computed before anything happens, so a value AWS invents is a blank in it.

choices.text: The provider hides values that come from other resources
choices.why: Nothing is hidden; the value simply does not exist at plan time.

choices.text: moto does not report VPC ids during a plan
choices.why: Against real AWS the plan shows the same thing: there is no VPC to report.

prompt: Ana's second apply ran after the four resources existed, with `main.tf` unchanged. How many resources did it add?
hint: Read its last line.

prompt: `terraform apply` shows the plan and asks. Ana types `y` and presses Enter. What happens?
hint: The question says what it accepts.

choices.text: The apply is cancelled
choices.why: Right: only the exact word `yes` approves. Anything else cancels, as `no` did in the lesson.

choices.text: The four resources are created, since `y` is short for yes
choices.why: Terraform does not accept abbreviations here, on purpose.

choices.text: Terraform asks the same question again
choices.why: It does not repeat the question; the run ends with `Apply cancelled.`

choices.text: Only the VPC is created, as a partial approval
choices.why: There is no partial approval: the plan is accepted whole or not at all.

prompt: Put these steps of the first apply in the order the log shows them finishing.
hint: Follow the arrows of the graph.
trap: The plan lists the rule last too, but for another reason: the plan is alphabetical, the apply follows the graph.

prompt: `terraform.tfvars` says `environment = "dev"`. Ana runs `TF_VAR_environment=prod terraform plan`. Which value does the plan use?
hint: Where does the environment come in Terraform's order?

choices.text: `prod`, because an environment variable overrides a file
choices.why: That is how many tools behave, and it is the reverse of Terraform's order.

choices.text: Neither: two values for one variable are an error
choices.why: No error and no warning: one source simply wins.

choices.text: Terraform asks which one Ana meant
choices.why: It asks only when there is no value at all.

choices.text: `dev`, the value the file holds
choices.why: Right. `TF_VAR_` is the weakest source; the lesson's console showed `prod` losing to the file, and only `-var` beat it.

prompt: `environment` has no default. A pipeline runs `terraform plan -input=false` without giving it a value. What happens?
hint: What does `-input=false` turn the question into?

choices.text: It plans with an empty string
choices.why: A required variable has no fallback; an empty string would be a value somebody chose.

choices.text: The plan fails with `No value for required variable`
choices.why: Yes, naming the variable and the line that declared it, which is what you want where nobody can answer.

choices.text: It waits for somebody to type a value
choices.why: That is what happens in a terminal without `-input=false`.

choices.text: It skips the resources that use the variable
choices.why: Terraform does not plan half a configuration; it stops.

prompt: To give the variable `environment` a value through the shell, Ana exports a variable named ___.
hint: A fixed prefix, then the variable's name.

prompt: What does adding `default = 443` to the `https_port` variable change?
hint: Compare it with `environment`, which has none.

choices.text: It fixes the port at 443 so no file or flag can change it
choices.why: A default is used only when no source gives a value; `-var https_port=8443` would still win.

choices.text: It makes the variable optional
choices.why: Yes: with a default, Terraform neither asks nor fails when no value is given.

choices.text: It sets the variable's type to number
choices.why: The type comes from `type = number`; a default must fit it, but does not set it.

choices.text: It writes 443 into `terraform.tfvars`
choices.why: Terraform never edits your files; the default lives in the variable block.

prompt: A shell script needs the VPC's id as a bare string to pass to `aws ec2 describe-vpcs --vpc-ids`. Which command gives it?
hint: No quotes, no newline.

choices.text: `terraform output vpc_id`
choices.why: That prints the value in HCL syntax, with quotes the AWS CLI would receive as part of the id.

choices.text: `terraform output -json`
choices.why: That is for programs that parse JSON; a shell would get a whole document.

choices.text: `terraform output -raw vpc_id`
choices.why: Right: the bare string, which the lesson put inside `$( … )`.

choices.text: `grep vpc- terraform.tfstate`
choices.why: The state's layout is Terraform's business, and that grep matches more than one line.

prompt: Ana adds an `output "bucket_name"` block to `outputs.tf` and immediately runs `terraform output bucket_name`, without applying. What does she get?
hint: Where does `terraform output` read from?

choices.text: An error saying the output is not found, suggesting an apply
choices.why: Yes. Outputs come from the state, and only an apply writes a new one there.

choices.text: The bucket's name, computed from the files
choices.why: `terraform output` does not evaluate the files; it reads what the last apply stored.

choices.text: `(known after apply)`
choices.why: That marker belongs to a plan, not to `terraform output`.

choices.text: An empty line
choices.why: It fails with a message rather than printing nothing.

prompt: Match each command to what it prints.
hint: Three readers: a person, a shell, a program.

pairs.right: Every output, one `name = value` per line
One value in HCL syntax, quotes included
The bare string, without even a newline
Each output with its type and its sensitive flag

right_distractors: The ids read live from the AWS API

prompt: The mirror holds random 3.8.1 and 3.9.1, and nothing is locked yet. `versions.tf` asks for `version = "~> 3.8.0"`. Which version does `terraform init` install?
hint: With three numbers written, which one may grow?

choices.text: 3.9.1, the newest available
choices.why: `~> 3.8.0` stops below 3.9; that would be `~> 3.8`.

choices.text: None: `~>` needs an exact version that exists
choices.why: `~>` is a range, and 3.8.1 is inside it.

choices.text: 3.8.1, the newest the range allows
choices.why: Right: only the patch may grow, so 3.8.1 is the newest version the range allows, as the lock file showed.

choices.text: 3.8.0, the version written in the constraint
choices.why: The constraint is a lower bound, not a pin, and 3.8.0 is not in the mirror anyway.

prompt: Ana changes random's constraint from `~> 3.8.0` to `~> 3.9`, and `terraform plan` refuses with `Inconsistent dependency lock file`. What does she run?
hint: The locked 3.8.1 is outside the new range.

choices.text: Delete `.terraform/` and plan again
choices.why: The disagreement is with the lock file, which is still there and still says 3.8.1.

choices.text: `terraform init -upgrade`
choices.why: Yes. It chooses again inside every constraint and rewrites the lock file, which a reviewer then sees in the diff.

choices.text: `terraform plan -upgrade`
choices.why: plan does not install providers; choosing versions is init's job.

choices.text: `terraform apply`, which installs what the plan needs
choices.why: apply refuses for the same reason plan did.

prompt: The bucket's name is `shop-assets-` followed by `random_id.bucket.hex`. Why does the name not change on every plan?
hint: Where does random keep what it drew?

choices.text: The value is drawn once, at creation, and kept in the state
choices.why: Right, and it stays until the resource is destroyed; that is the point of making it a resource.

choices.text: random asks AWS which suffixes are free
choices.why: The random provider calls nothing outside itself.

choices.text: The suffix is derived from the VPC id
choices.why: Nothing in `storage.tf` connects the two.

choices.text: The lock file records the suffix
choices.why: The lock file records provider versions and hashes, never resource values.

prompt: After `terraform destroy` finished, what was in `terraform.tfstate`?
hint: Ana asked `jq` for the length of `resources`.

choices.text: The file had been deleted along with the resources
choices.why: `ls` still listed it; destroy does not delete the state.

choices.text: The seven resources, marked as destroyed
choices.why: Destroyed resources leave the state; nothing is kept as a tombstone.

choices.text: The state, still there, recording zero resources
choices.why: Yes: a record that this configuration manages nothing right now.

choices.text: The previous state, renamed to `.backup`
choices.why: The backup is a separate file beside it; `terraform.tfstate` itself remained, empty of resources.

prompt: Which of these did Ana's `terraform destroy` delete? Choose all that apply.
hint: Seven resources, three providers.

choices.text: The VPC in moto
choices.why: Yes, last, once nothing inside it was left.

choices.text: `network.env` on the laptop
choices.why: Yes: destroying a `local_file` deletes the file.

choices.text: `main.tf`
choices.why: The configuration is untouched; the next plan read it and proposed seven creations.

choices.text: The `shop-assets-` bucket
choices.why: Yes; `aws s3 ls` listed nothing afterwards.

choices.text: `.terraform.lock.hcl`
choices.why: The lock file and `.terraform/` stay, so nothing needs installing again.

prompt: A colleague created a VPC by hand in the same account, tagged `Name = shop`. What does Ana's `terraform destroy` do to it?
hint: What does destroy read to decide what to remove?

choices.text: Deletes it, since its tag matches the configuration
choices.why: Terraform does not match resources by tag; it knows them by the ids in its state.

choices.text: Leaves it in place, since that VPC is not in Ana's state
choices.why: Right. It is not in the state, so destroy does not know it exists.

choices.text: Refuses to run until the extra VPC is imported
choices.why: Destroy never looks for resources it does not track; importing is lesson 8's subject.

choices.text: Adopts it into the state in place of the destroyed one
choices.why: Nothing is adopted automatically; the state only holds what this configuration created or imported.

prompt: Put the life of the shop's network in this lesson in order.
hint: Nothing runs before the providers are installed.
trap: Asking for an output before the apply is the usual slip: outputs are read from the state, which only an apply writes.

prompt: A colleague clones Ana's repository, which has the `.tf` files and the lock file but, as intended, no `.terraform/`, and runs `terraform plan` straight away. What happens?
hint: The lock file names versions; it does not contain programs.

choices.text: The plan runs, because the lock file pins every provider
choices.why: Pinning a version is not installing it; the program is still missing.

choices.text: Terraform downloads the locked versions as part of the plan
choices.why: plan never installs anything; that is init's job alone.

choices.text: It refuses until `terraform init` installs the providers
choices.why: Right. A fresh checkout always needs init, which will then install exactly the locked versions.

choices.text: It proposes creating the whole network a second time
choices.why: It never gets as far as a plan; and that risk is about the state, lesson 7's subject.

prompt: Ana wants to plan production from this directory, which keeps `terraform.tfvars` with `environment = "dev"`. She has `export TF_VAR_environment=prod` in her shell. What makes the plan use `prod`?
hint: Command-line values are the strongest source.

choices.text: Nothing more: the export already does it
choices.why: The export is the weakest source; the file wins, and the plan says `dev`.

choices.text: Running `terraform init` again, so the export is read
choices.why: init does not read variable values; the order of sources is the same after it.

choices.text: `-var-file=prod.tfvars` on the command line
choices.why: Yes. A file named on the command line beats `terraform.tfvars`, and the choice is visible in the command itself.

choices.text: Renaming the variable to `TF_VAR_environment` in `variables.tf`
choices.why: The prefix belongs to the shell variable, not to the declaration; the variable would no longer be `var.environment`.

prompt: Which of these edits make `terraform plan` refuse until Ana runs `init` (with or without `-upgrade`)? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether the lock file still agrees with `required_providers`.

choices.text: A second `aws_subnet` resource
choices.why: The aws provider is installed already; a new resource of a known type needs no init.

choices.text: A `tls` provider added to `required_providers`
choices.why: Yes: a provider with no version selected, as `random` and `local` were.

choices.text: A new output
choices.why: Outputs involve no provider; apply records them.

choices.text: A constraint the locked version falls outside
choices.why: Yes: `Inconsistent dependency lock file`, until `init -upgrade` chooses again.

choices.text: A variable with a default
choices.why: Variables are read at plan time; nothing needs installing.
